question: How does the pH scale work?

scenes.original_narration: Because the scale is logarithmic, equal steps in pH represent equal powers of ten in hydronium concentration. Lower pH means more H₃O⁺ and an acidic solution. Higher pH means less H₃O⁺; when hydronium is lower than hydroxide, the solution is basic. Therefore, pH is not a linear ruler.
scenes.replacement_narration: Because the scale is logarithmic, equal steps in pH represent equal powers of ten in hydronium concentration. A lower pH means a greater hydronium concentration. A solution is acidic when hydronium concentration is greater than hydroxide concentration, and basic when it is lower. So pH is not a linear ruler.

scenes.original_narration: Neutrality is defined by equal hydronium and hydroxide concentrations. In the supplied chart at 25 °C, pure water is marked pH 7 and neutral. The chart classifies solutions with greater hydronium than hydroxide as acidic, and those with less hydronium as basic. Thus, the pH 7 statement here is specifically a 25 °C reference.

This balanced diagram shows equal concentrations of the two ions. The temperature qualification matters: pH seven here is specifically the neutral reference at twenty-five degrees Celsius.

Increasing pH by one therefore means a tenfold decrease in hydronium concentration in this comparison. Moving toward pH 7 is a substantial concentration change, not one small linear step.

A 0–14 strip is a common display, but it is not a universal bound: the supplied chart also includes pH −1 and pH 15. The core rule remains unchanged: lower pH means greater hydronium concentration.

narration.title: What pH Measures
narration.narration: pH tells us about the molar concentration of hydronium ions in an aqueous solution. The definition is pH equals negative log, base ten, of hydronium concentration. The brackets mean concentration. So pH is not a direct concentration number; it is a compact logarithmic way to report it.
